lines.text: How many times does a coin turn when it rolls around another one?
Two identical coins on a table. One stays still.
The other rolls around it, pressed against its edge, without slipping a single millimeter, until it's back where it started.
It sounds like a silly question. How many times did the rolling coin turn around itself?
Well, in 1982, this exact question broke an official exam.
Almost everyone says one. And the reasoning looks perfect.
The two coins are identical, so they have the same edge.
Roll along a whole edge, and you make exactly one turn.
It's so clean you don't even stop to check it.
It's two.
Watch the arrow.
Halfway around, the coin is on the far side, and the arrow is already pointing up again.
One full turn, with only half the trip done. By the time it gets back, that's two.
The trick is in where you're looking.
It's not the point where they touch that matters. It's the center.
The center of the rolling coin never gets any closer. It always stays two radii away from the other one.
So it doesn't travel around the edge of the still coin. It travels around a circle twice as big.
Twice the distance means two turns.
There's another way to see it, and it's my favorite.
Unroll the still coin into a straight line, and roll the other one along it.
It makes exactly one turn. One.
But the real track isn't straight. It's a circle, and going all the way around it swings the coin through another three hundred sixty degrees on its own.
Rolling gives you one turn. Going around gives you the other.
And this isn't just a coin trick. It happens to you every day.
The Earth spins about three hundred sixty-six times a year, but you only count three hundred sixty-five days.
The orbit eats that extra spin. The Earth rolls around the Sun just like one coin around the other.
And now, back to 1982.
On the SAT, the American college entrance exam, this question showed up with a circle three times bigger.
The right answer was four. The rule is the ratio of the sizes, plus one.
But look at the answer choices. Four wasn't there.
Three students caught it and wrote in. The question was thrown out, and around three hundred thousand exams had to be rescored.
And the best part: you don't have to take my word for it. It's in your pocket.
Take two identical coins, watch the face on one, and roll it around the other without letting it slip. Count the turns.
If you get two, tell me in the comments. If you get one, you let it slip.
And you, what did you answer before you saw it?
